summary: Every mechanical guard that protects this repository, and the stage each one runs in. This file is the single source of truth: scripts/audit-guards.mjs proves every entry is real and every stage claim is true, docs/guards.md explains them, and /guards renders them.

stages.title: Prebuild
stages.description: Runs before any bundle is produced. These guards regenerate the page index and then immediately re-audit it, so a page can never be advertised and unreachable in the same build.

stages.title: Gate
stages.when: `npm run gate`, before you call a feature done.
stages.description: The composite correctness sweep: the CLAUDE.md truth check, the critical-path tests, and every offline audit. Ordered cheapest first, so a merge-conflict marker fails in seconds instead of after the test stage.

stages.title: Deploy build
stages.when: `npm run build:gcp`, before an image is submitted to Cloud Build.
stages.description: Guards that can only judge a finished artifact: the browser bundle, the contents of dist/, and whether every declared page actually resolves against the route table.

stages.title: Pre-push
stages.description: Installed into .git/hooks by scripts/setup-git-hooks.mjs on every npm install. Judges exactly the commits leaving the machine and never the shared working tree, so a concurrent agent's in-flight edit can never block your push. Bypass once with SKIP_PUSH_CHECKS=1.

stages.title: On demand
stages.when: Run it yourself when you touch the area it covers.
stages.description: Guards that need a browser, live credentials, or a network round trip, so they cannot sit on an automatic path without making it flaky. Each one has an npm script so it is discoverable rather than buried in scripts/.

guards.title: Merge-conflict markers
guards.protects: No unresolved conflict marker can be built or deployed.
guards.why: A stash-pop conflict was once committed wholesale and reached production source. A conflict marker is a syntax error rather than a lint violation, so neither eslint nor vitest caught it. It runs first in both chains because it costs seconds and the build costs minutes.

proof.summary: A staged source file carrying an unresolved conflict marker.

guards.title: CLAUDE.md truth check
guards.protects: Every script, path, count, and runbook step named in CLAUDE.md matches the repo.
guards.why: Agents execute CLAUDE.md verbatim, so a stale line does not read as stale, it reads as an instruction. Each claim is re-derived from its source of truth on every run: the cron count from vercel.json, the deploy chain order from the real npm script, the documented git remotes from git itself.

proof.summary: CLAUDE.md telling an agent to run an npm script that does not exist.

append.CLAUDE.md: Proof fixture: verify the toolchain with `npm run guard-proof-nonexistent`.

guards.title: Vendored worker modules stay identical
guards.protects: Every copy of a shared worker module (worker_security.py, oin.py, oin_upload.py, gltf_meshopt.py and its test) is byte-identical across all workers.
guards.why: A worker's Docker build context is its own directory, so `../` is unreachable and shared code lives as a copy in each worker that needs it. Nothing enforced that, so a fix applied to one copy could leave the other sixteen on the old behaviour, which is the shape of bug this repo has already paid for once. The guard compares every copy against the most common one and names the divergent files and the command that resyncs them.

proof.summary: One worker's copy of worker_security.py edited so it no longer matches the other sixteen.

append.workers/stylize/worker_security.py: # Proof fixture: this line exists in one copy only, so the copies have drifted.

guards.title: 3D Studio OpenAPI sync
guards.protects: The custom-GPT Actions file in the OpenAI submission kit is byte-identical to the OpenAPI schema three.ws actually serves.
guards.why: The served schema at public/.well-known/3d-studio-openapi.yaml is what https://three.ws/.well-known/3d-studio-openapi.yaml returns and what the GPT builder imports by URL, while prompts/store-submissions/_generated/openai-actions.yaml is the copy an OpenAI reviewer reads. Two hand-maintained copies of one contract drift, and the drift shows up as a reviewer reading a document the runtime does not serve. The served file is the source of truth and the copy is regenerated from it.

proof.summary: The submission kit shipping an Actions contract that no longer matches the schema the site serves.

append.public/.well-known/3d-studio-openapi.yam: # drift fixture: served schema edited without regenerating the submission copy

guards.title: Hard rules, diff scoped
guards.protects: The CLAUDE.md hard rules on the lines you actually changed.
guards.why: A repo-wide sweep is impossible because thousands of tracked files predate the rules. Reading added lines only stops the bleeding without rewriting history: your change is held to the bar, the legacy around it is left alone. It also synthesizes hunks for untracked files, which a bare git diff cannot see.

proof.summary: A new source file whose added lines break a CLAUDE.md hard rule.

guards.title: Credential material, before it leaves the machine
guards.protects: No dotenv file, private key, keystore, or downloaded cloud credential becomes a tracked file, and no added line carries a provider-issued key.
guards.why: A leaked key in git is not a bug you fix by deleting the line: every clone, fork, and mirror keeps a copy, so the only real remedy is rotating the credential at the provider. That asymmetry is why it runs before the push rather than after. Filenames are judged repo-wide and absolutely (the tree holds zero of them, so there is no legacy to grandfather); contents are judged diff scoped, because a repo-wide content scan drowns in hex addresses and placeholder docs until someone switches it off.

proof.summary: An SSH private key staged as a tracked file.

write.id_ed25519: not a real key: the filename alone is what this guard judges

guards.title: Cron schedule drift
guards.protects: Every cron declared in vercel.json is a valid expression, and matches what Cloud Scheduler is actually running.
guards.why: vercel.json is a live config file: the scheduler sync seeds Cloud Scheduler from its crons array. A schedule edited without a re-sync, or a job paused by hand during an incident and never resumed, fails silently because the declared config still looks right. The offline half validates expressions and runs in the gate; the live half compares against the running jobs.

proof.reason: Compares the crons declared in vercel.json against the jobs actually deployed to Cloud Scheduler, so it needs an authenticated gcloud session and the live project. There is nothing offline to mutate.

guards.title: Route documentation
guards.protects: Every human-facing route in vercel.json is documented in data/pages.json.
guards.why: data/pages.json feeds the sitemap, llms.txt, features.json, and the changelog. A page missing from it is invisible to crawlers and to the changelog, so it ships without ever being announced.

proof.summary: A public page route in vercel.json that no data/pages.json entry documents.

guards.title: Declared pages resolve
guards.protects: Every page declared in data/pages.json is actually reachable.
guards.why: Anything listed in pages.json is advertised to crawlers the moment it lands. Two pages shipped as hard 404s in three days, each with a built dist file and no route rewrite. The local mode gates the deploy build; the base-url mode sweeps a live deployment after it.

proof.summary: A page advertised in data/pages.json with no built file behind it.

guards.title: Routing and 404 model
guards.protects: Every catalog page is reachable, unknown paths reach the designed 404, and no page route is shadowed by an earlier rule.
guards.why: The route table is evaluated in order and split at the filesystem marker, so an earlier catch-all can swallow a later literal route. A handler can be routed and still never run, which is invisible until someone reports the endpoint dead.

proof.summary: Deleting the route that serves a catalogued page, so its pretty URL 404s.

guards.title: API handlers export a body
guards.protects: No API handler ships as an empty file or without an export.
guards.why: The api tree uses a dispatcher-shim pattern where a real endpoint can be a one-line re-export, which makes an accidentally empty handler look normal in review and return nothing in production.

proof.summary: An API file that is routable but exports nothing, so it can never serve a response.

guards.title: The [hidden] guard
guards.protects: Every page resolves the CSS that makes the hidden attribute actually hide.
guards.why: The hidden HTML attribute only hides an element while some stylesheet maps it. A page that misses that rule renders its hidden scaffolding to real users. This is the verifier half of an inject-and-audit pair.

proof.summary: A product page that links no shared stylesheet, so [hidden] never hides anything.

guards.title: CSP-safe inline markup
guards.protects: No served HTML carries an inline event handler attribute or a javascript: URL.
guards.why: server/csp-hashes.mjs replaced script-src 'unsafe-inline' with the SHA-256 hashes of the inline <script> blocks in each response. A hash covers a script element and nothing else, so an onclick= attribute or a javascript: href needs 'unsafe-hashes' to run, which hands the mitigation straight back. Reintroducing one does not fail any build or test on its own: it simply stops working in production while passing locally, because a dev server without the header runs it fine.

proof.summary: A page wiring a click through an onclick attribute, which no script hash can cover.

guards.title: Live CSP sweep
guards.protects: No page violates the Content-Security-Policy the server sends with it.
guards.why: server/csp-hashes.mjs derives script-src from the bytes of each response, which is a strong guarantee on paper and a total outage when it is wrong: one missed inline script ships that page blank. Only a browser applies a policy the way a browser applies a policy, so this loads the real pages against a running server and fails on any securitypolicyviolation event. Add --all to sweep every route in data/pages.json.

proof.reason: Needs Playwright plus a server serving dist/, because the thing under test is the browser's own policy evaluation against a real response. A static fixture cannot produce a securitypolicyviolation event.

guards.title: Documentation integrity
guards.protects: No dead relative link, no site link that matches no route, no command naming a script that no longer exists, and no packages or workers directory without a README.
guards.why: Docs rot silently: a page gets renamed, a script gets dropped, a directory moves, and the doc that pointed at it keeps looking correct. Renaming or deleting a file is exactly when this earns its keep.

proof.summary: A doc whose relative link points at a file that does not exist.

guards.title: Tutorial reachability
guards.protects: Every tutorial appears in the library manifest, has its markdown on disk, and is registered in data/pages.json, with no duplicate slugs.

Run it with --write to register what is missing.

guards.title: MCP tool catalog freshness
guards.protects: public/mcp-catalog.json matches what the MCP servers actually expose.
guards.why: The searchable tool index at /mcp-tools renders from the generated catalog. A stale catalog advertises tools that moved, renamed, or no longer exist, which is worse than advertising nothing.

proof.summary: A new MCP tool landing without regenerating the public catalog.

guards.title: x402 endpoint catalog
guards.protects: Every paid endpoint under api/x402 is documented in the public catalog.
guards.why: Each paid endpoint is a sellable product an agent can discover and call. One that exists but is undocumented earns nothing, because no buyer can find it.

proof.summary: A paid x402 endpoint that no buyer can find, because the catalog never mentions it.

guards.title: MCP manifests
guards.protects: Every MCP registry manifest satisfies the official registry's rules, offline.
guards.why: The official registry enforces these rules at publish time, so a manifest that drifts past them blocks the next publish instead of failing here, where it is cheap to fix.

proof.summary: A registry manifest whose description exceeds the 100-character schema limit.

json.set: A deliberately overlong registry description used by the guard proof sandbox to exceed the one hundred character schema limit imposed by the registry.

guards.title: MCP golden contracts
guards.protects: Tool names, descriptions, annotations, and input schemas of every hosted MCP server, against a committed snapshot.
guards.why: That contract is what external agents integrate against, so a well-meaning description edit silently changes how other people's agents route. It parses the sources statically rather than importing them, because importing would pull in database and RPC clients.

proof.summary: A tool contract appearing on the wire without being declared in the golden fixture.

guards.title: MCP safety annotations
guards.protects: Every MCP tool's declared safety annotations match what its handler actually does.
guards.why: Annotations are not decoration: clients read readOnlyHint and destructiveHint to decide what may run without asking a human. A tool that writes while claiming to be read-only removes a confirmation the user was relying on.

proof.summary: A tool shipping with no safety annotations at all, so a client cannot judge it.

guards.title: Design-token ratchet
guards.protects: Hardcoded colour hexes cannot creep back past a committed baseline.
guards.why: public/tokens.css is the single source of truth for colour primitives, but a big-bang cleanup of every legacy hex is not possible. Counting violations against a baseline and failing only when the count rises makes the debt strictly decreasing.

proof.summary: A token-covered page hardcoding a hex that is literally a design token.

write.pages/guard-proof-token.html: fixture

guards.title: Browser bundle purity
guards.protects: No Node-only module leaks into the browser bundle.
guards.why: A Node builtin pulled into browser code does not fail the build, it fails at runtime in the user's tab, usually on a page nobody tested after the import was added.

proof.summary: A Node built-in reaching the browser bundle through a real import chain.

append.src/solana/sns.js:
import { promisify } from 'node:util';
export const proofPromisify = promisify;

guards.title: Bootstrap ordering
guards.protects: No page calls its own entry point above the state that entry point writes.
guards.why: JavaScriptCore checks an assignment target's temporal dead zone before it evaluates the right-hand side and V8 checks it afterwards, so a module that bootstraps itself above its own `let`s renders correctly in Chrome and throws "Cannot access uninitialized variable." in every Safari. That shipped: each /avatars/:id page was dead on iOS and macOS while review, the page audit and the production smoke sweep all stayed green, because every one of them looks only at V8. A synchronous read of a later-declared binding is worse still and throws everywhere.

proof.summary: A page whose top-level bootstrap writes a `let` declared further down the module.

guards.title: Build output shape
guards.protects: dist/ contains every artifact the deploy expects, including the UMD library bundle.
guards.why: The frontend build empties dist/, so anything written before it is destroyed. This fails the build when the order was wrong instead of shipping an image missing its pages or its library.

proof.summary: A build that finished without producing the published embed bundle.

guards.title: Deploy artifact preflight
guards.protects: The two artifact failure classes that have taken production down.
guards.why: Both are invisible in a diff and obvious in seconds if something looks. Running it before a submit costs nothing next to a failed Cloud Build.

proof.summary: A symlink committed to the index, which the deploy bundler cannot resolve.

guards.title: Cloud Build upload contents
guards.protects: What `gcloud builds submit` would actually upload.
guards.why: An over-broad ignore file silently drops a file the build needs; an under-broad one uploads gigabytes of node_modules and times out. Neither is visible until the build runs.

proof.summary: A missing .gcloudignore, which silently hands the upload set back to .gitignore.

guards.title: Site link integrity
guards.protects: Every navigable target across pages, public, and src resolves to a real route or file.
guards.why: It resolves each link against the real routing model rather than assuming the catch-all rules count as proof, so a dead internal path cannot hide behind a wildcard that would serve a 404 page.

proof.summary: A route in vercel.json whose destination file was never created.

guards.title: Console sweep
guards.protects: A clean browser console on every canonical route, at desktop and mobile widths.
guards.why: A clean console is part of the definition of done, and the only way to prove it is to drive the real pages in a real browser. Environment noise is filtered so the output is signal.

proof.reason: Drives a real browser over the live page set and reads the console, so it needs Playwright and a running server. A static fixture cannot produce a runtime console error.

guards.title: Image loading attributes
guards.protects: Every JS-rendered image sets its loading and decoding attributes.
guards.why: These images pull remote thumbnails and avatars. Without the attributes the browser blocks rendering on images far below the fold, which shows up as a slow page rather than as an error.

proof.summary: A JS-rendered image with no loading attribute, which fetches eagerly off-screen.

guards.title: Wardrobe catalog integrity
guards.protects: Every garment in the live catalog validates, and its GLB hash matches its manifest.
guards.why: It runs the same validation the closet runs at consume time, against the real fetched asset, so a re-uploaded or corrupted GLB is caught before a user wears it.

proof.reason: Fetches every published garment asset over the network and inspects the returned GLB, so there is no offline input to mutate.

guards.title: Rig coverage
guards.protects: How well the canonicalizer maps the skeletons actually stored in production.
guards.why: The bone-name tables grew by anticipating rig conventions, and anticipation is not evidence. This walks real avatars and ranks the unmapped bone names by frequency, so the next mapping to add is a measurement rather than a guess.

proof.reason: Loads real avatar rigs from production storage and retargets clips onto them, which needs live credentials and the model bucket.

guards.title: Service wallet configuration
guards.protects: Every platform wallet's on-chain balance, its floor, and whether the advertised x402 fee payer matches the secret we actually co-sign with.
guards.why: An advertised fee-payer that does not match the configured secret silently 502s paid endpoints, and a wallet under its floor pauses its engine. Both look identical from outside and have different fixes.

proof.reason: Reads live balances for the service wallets over RPC using the production keys in .env.

guards.title: Fleet wallet flows
guards.protects: Where the platform's SOL is, where it has been going, and whether any of it is leaking.
guards.why: Every time the paid rail goes dry the first theory is a leak. This separates the three real answers by measurement: capital dispersed into agent wallets, a starved fee floor, and an actual unexplained debit.

proof.reason: Reconstructs on-chain transfer history for the fleet wallets from live RPC, so it has no offline input.

guards.title: LLM spend metering
guards.protects: Every LLM lane that spends money reports a real cost, never exactly $0 and never an unknown.
guards.why: A cost lane reporting zero is worse than one reporting nothing: it reads as free traffic. OpenRouter was on the blanket free-provider list while the platform key routed paid vendor mirrors, so a real $30 balance drained with the dashboard showing $0 the whole way down, and nobody noticed until the key stopped working.

proof.reason: Aggregates the usage_events ledger over a time window, so it has no offline input. The rule it applies is unit-tested without a database in tests/llm-metering-rule.test.js.

guards.title: Relayer balances
guards.protects: Every configured Solana signer is above its documented minimum.
guards.why: The operator companion to the balance watchdog cron, run on demand from a machine that holds the signer secrets. Unconfigured signers are listed explicitly so the real deployment's holdings are visible at a glance.

proof.reason: Queries the funded relayer accounts over RPC and compares them against the operating floor, which only exists on-chain.

guards.title: The guard registry itself
guards.protects: Every entry in this file names a real script and a real npm script, every guard on disk is registered, and every stage claim matches the npm chain that would actually run it.
guards.why: This registry is rendered by docs/guards.md and by /guards, so a stale stage column does not read as stale, it reads as coverage a reader then stops looking for. Listing itself is not circular: it verifies its own script, npm binding, and gate membership exactly like every other entry.

proof.summary: A registry entry naming a guard script that is not in the repository.

guards.title: Delegation contract addresses
guards.protects: Every address in the delegation-manager deployment table is a deployed contract on its chain.
guards.why: A wrong or undeployed address fails only at the moment a user signs, which is the worst possible time to discover a typo in a constant.

proof.reason: Resolves the delegation-framework contract addresses against live chain RPC, so the values it compares only exist on-chain.

guards.title: Overlapping fixed overlays
guards.protects: No persistent floating widget can cover another one's controls.
guards.why: Viewport-anchored UI accumulated independently: the walk companion, the corner stack, consent bars, sticky rails, the chat launcher. Each is correct alone and they compete for the same few hundred pixels. The collision only appears on the one page where both are mounted at the one viewport where they touch, which is invisible to unit tests and to whoever built either widget. Every earlier fix was a bug report plus a hand measurement plus a magic offset.

proof.reason: Drives a real Chromium over real routes at real viewports and measures painted geometry, so the input is a rendered page rather than a file a fixture could write.

guards.title: Runnable doc samples still answer
guards.protects: Every sample a reader can press Run on still returns what the doc says it returns.
guards.why: A curl command in a tutorial can point at an endpoint renamed two quarters ago and nothing notices, because the doc still reads fine. This executes each sample through the same extractor the page uses (public/runnable-extract.js), so the doc and the check can never disagree about what the sample is.

proof.reason: Executes the documented calls against the live API and compares real response statuses, so there is no offline input to mutate.

guards.title: Doc figures match their manifest
guards.protects: Every figure a doc points at was really captured, still matches its recipe, and carries alt text.
guards.why: The capture pipeline can produce a correct image while the docs stay wrong: a tutorial points at a file nobody captured, a recipe outlives the doc that used it, an image gets swapped by hand so it no longer matches what the caption claims, or it ships with no alt text, which is a defect for every reader on a screen reader. None of that is visible in a diff.

proof.summary: A doc figure whose image file does not exist on disk.

# Proof fixture

![a figure that was never captured](/docs/img/guard-proof-missing.png)

guards.title: Live event window
guards.protects: public/event.json describes an event that will actually happen, on every surface that reads it.
guards.why: One file drives the /play lobby banner, the in-world countdown and meetup layer, the game server's quest gate, the leaderboard endpoints and the souvenir grant. Every one of them treats a bad or expired window as 'there is no event' and mounts nothing, so the failure is silent and total: the page loads, the world runs, and the entire event is simply absent with no error to say why. That has already happened once, when a rehearsal window was left in the file.

proof.summary: An event window whose end has already passed, which every surface reads as 'no event' and mounts nothing.

guards.title: The tour atlas tells the truth
guards.protects: public/tour/atlas.json matches a fresh render of data/tour-atlas.json: every stop resolves, every screenshot it promises exists on disk, and the curated anchors still parse.
guards.why: The atlas is a committed snapshot of a capture run. Edit the source manifest without re-rendering, delete a screenshot, or rot an anchor selector and the /tour-atlas page keeps promising media and spotlight targets that no longer exist. None of that fails a build on its own; only re-deriving the atlas and comparing catches it.

proof.reason: The check re-renders the committed atlas from data/tour-atlas.json and verifies 160 captured screenshots exist on disk; a sandbox proof would need the full media tree copied per run, so it is exercised by the real gate instead.

guards.title: No API handler is routed but unreachable
guards.protects: Every handler under api/ that looks routed can actually be reached, by replaying the production router's ordered walk of vercel.json against each handler's own canonical URL.
guards.why: The route table is evaluated in order, so an earlier catch-all such as /api/agents/([^/]+) swallows every literal sibling declared after it. The handler file exists, the route table appears to mention it, and the endpoint is simply dead: it returns another handler's answer. This is invisible in a diff and in local testing, and has silently killed documented endpoints before. verify-routes covers PAGE routes; this covers API handlers.

proof.reason: The audit currently reports a real backlog of 46 shadowed handlers, so it exits non-zero against the live repo and cannot yet pass the control half of a sandboxed proof. It stays a manual audit until that backlog is cleared, at which point it can move into the gate with a two-sided proof.

guards.title: Every declared cron is actually alive
guards.protects: Each cron in vercel.json resolves through the real route table to a handler file that exists, imports without throwing, answers a live request, and refuses an unauthenticated one.
guards.why: check-cron-drift answers 'is the schedule valid and is Cloud Scheduler running it?', which a silently dead cron passes: the job shows ENABLED, the schedule matches, the request lands, and the server 404s it or imports a handler that throws at module scope. Nothing anywhere notices. That exact gap killed all 30+ dispatcher jobs (payouts, subscriptions, buybacks, pumpfun monitors) until July 2026, because vercel.json's legacy routes array does not auto-route the [name] dynamic segment. This walks route, handler, load, and run per cron, and reports a cron that answers 200 without a bearer token as UNGATED rather than as a pass.

proof.reason: The run stage boots the real server on a free port and probes every cron URL, so the check is inherently live. The probe is deliberately unauthenticated and every handler fails closed on CRON_SECRET, so no job body executes: nothing is paid, swapped, minted, transferred, or written. `--static` skips the boot for a route-and-load-only pass.

guards.title: No custodial SOL is stranded behind an unreadable key
guards.protects: Every stored custodial Solana secret still decrypts under the current WALLET_ENCRYPTION_KEY, and reports the SOL sitting behind any that do not.
guards.why: The treasury self-heal reclaims idle SOL from platform-owned agent wallets when the master fee wallet runs short. A wallet whose encrypted_solana_secret fails AES-GCM decryption cannot be signed for, so its balance is invisible to that self-heal and to every other spend path, and the failure is silent by construction: the reclaim leg reports a failed SEND, and a WebCrypto OperationError wearing a Solana costume sends operators after RPC health and funding for a key problem neither can fix. A key rotation is the usual cause; the WALLET_ENCRYPTION_KEY changed during the 2026-07 Vercel to Cloud Run migration and every wallet written under the retired key became unreadable.

proof.reason: It reads the production wallet table and the live encryption key, then decrypts in memory to test each secret against the current key. There is no offline fixture for 'this ciphertext no longer opens' that would prove anything about the real fleet. Read-only: it never writes, signs, or broadcasts.

guards.title: No connected home is sealed behind an unreadable key
guards.protects: Every stored Home Assistant long-lived token still decrypts under the current WALLET_ENCRYPTION_KEY, and names the homes that would go dark if one does not.
guards.why: home_connections.access_token_enc is the platform second class of at-rest ciphertext under the same key as the custodial wallet secrets, and a rotation that loses the outgoing value seals both. The two failures look nothing alike, which is why one reading cannot cover both: a sealed wallet strands SOL that can never be signed for again, while a sealed home token strands nothing and costs reach. Every connected house simply stops answering at once, with no balance anywhere to notice it by and no signal that says why, until each owner pastes a fresh token. Run it beside the wallet audit on every key rotation.

proof.reason: It reads the production home_connections table and the live encryption key, then decrypts in memory to test each token against the current key. There is no offline fixture for "this ciphertext no longer opens" that would prove anything about the real fleet. Read-only: it never writes and never opens a socket to any house.

guards.title: Hands-free voice loop
guards.protects: The browser voice loop keeps the properties the feature is sold on: nothing about listening loads before opt-in, an ambient "yeah" never confirms a guarded action, and the agent does not wake itself.
guards.why: This loop holds a live microphone and can reach a physical actuator, so its claims are the kind that have to be measured rather than reasoned about. It drives a real Chromium with a fake capture device fed from speech the platform synthesized itself, and walks ten scenarios end to end including barge-in, mute at the track, a refused microphone and a deployment with no speech lane. It cannot sit on an automatic path: it needs a browser, a server and the live speech lanes, and a flaky guard on the gate is a guard people learn to skip.

proof.reason: Drives a real Chromium against the running voice loop with a synthesized microphone stream. The behaviours under test (a wake word firing, playback stopping on barge-in, a capture track actually ending) only exist at runtime, so there is no static fixture that could stand in for them.

guards.title: /play failure-mode audit
guards.protects: /play stays usable when its dependencies fail, and hostile deep-link params never execute.
guards.why: The clean-path console audit proves nothing about the paths an event crowd actually hits: no session, an ad blocker eating IPFS, a dead GLB, a 500 on the auth nonce, a pass that expires mid-session, a pasted link carrying hostile name/symbol/image params. Each scenario is injected in a real browser and the boot loader must always resolve, into the world or into a designed error card with a recovery action, never a stuck spinner.

proof.reason: Needs Playwright plus a running server, because the thing under test is how the page behaves when a specific request is aborted or rewritten mid-load. A static fixture cannot fail a fetch the page has not made yet.

guards.title: No outbound call without a deadline
guards.protects: Every fetch to a third-party host is bounded, so one stalled upstream cannot hold a request open until the platform kills it.
guards.why: A fetch with no signal has no deadline at all: undici's defaults run to minutes, so an upstream that accepts a connection and then stalls holds the whole invocation and takes the request budget of every fallback behind it. From the outside that is not a slow provider, it is a dead endpoint, a dead cron, or a page that spins forever. Only the deadline is enforced, because retries, provider ladders and last-good tiers are judgement calls per call site while a deadline never is. The checker balances parentheses to read each call's real extent, since signal is conventionally the last key of an options object and a fixed window would report a bounded call as unbounded exactly when its options are longest.

proof.summary: A fetch to a third-party host added with no signal and no bounding wrapper.

guards.title: The iOS app icon still is the brand mark
guards.protects: The committed app icon and launch images are exactly what the current brand mark produces, and the icon carries no alpha channel.
guards.why: The iOS icon is the one asset that cannot be generated at build time: it is compiled into the .ipa from Assets.xcassets, so whatever is committed is what ships to every home screen. Both failure modes are silent. A hand-exported replacement drifts away from public/pwa-512x512.png and nothing anywhere notices, so the app wears a stale mark for a release cycle. And an icon that reaches App Store Connect with an alpha channel is rejected outright, which surfaces at upload time on someone else's Mac, hours after the change that caused it. Re-deriving the assets and comparing bytes catches both before either can leave the repository.

proof.summary: The committed app icon replaced with bytes the brand mark does not produce.

guards.title: Upstream resilience ratchet
guards.protects: No new call to a third-party service can be added without a deadline, and no existing one can quietly get weaker.
guards.why: Adding a fallback is easy; knowing it made things better is not. An AST pass grades every outbound call site on five protections (deadline, retry, failover, last-good, breaker) and compares it against data/upstream-baseline.json. A ratchet rather than a threshold: a threshold gets rounded up until it means nothing, while a baseline lets the existing tail be paid down at its own pace and makes adding to it by accident impossible. Improving a call site lowers the baseline automatically; raising it back needs an explicit --accept, which is one reviewable line in a diff. It measures what check:fetch-timeouts cannot: that guard enforces the deadline floor, this one measures everything above it.

proof.summary: A new outbound call to a third-party host with no deadline behind it.

exempt.reason: One-off integration verifiers for a specific vendor surface or world build, not repository guards. They prove an external service works, so they belong with that feature rather than in a guard stage.
